title: The trailing-slash matrix
description: One link, four combinations — why no fixed depth shift can be correct in both dev and production

artifact.purpose: Show the four dev/production × shift-off/shift-on combinations side by side, each traced from the address bar to the resolved URL, so the diagonal is visible at a glance rather than reconstructed from prose.

palette.note: No palette of its own — site mode. Pass/fail is carried by --color-success / --color-error; the neutral hex values written inline are the out-of-engine fallback layer only (#fafafa, #f5f5f5, #eeeeee, #1a1a1a, #525252, #737373, #e5e5e5, #f0f0f0, #2563eb, #16a34a, #dc2626, #ca8a04, #0891b2).

data.tree_state: Both attempts reverted — no shift, no trailingSlash. The top-left cell is what ships.
data.preview_equals_dev: 0 disagreements over 1245 links; dev vs a real file server: 546 disagreements

key_facts: A browser resolves a relative href against the directory portion of the current address; the trailing slash decides where that directory ends.
The two rows differ by exactly one URL segment — the same amount the shift changes — so no constant offset is correct in both, including zero.
astro dev and astro preview are route tables and never add the slash; a static host is a file server and always does, so dev-vs-preview tests one row twice.
The permanent fix is root-absolute resolution at render time; its one missing ingredient is the section base_url, which never reaches the parser layer.
